questions.q: During a site inspection, you notice that the contractor is about to pour concrete for a 2nd-floor cantilevered balcony. The 'rebar spacer blocks' (chairs) are missing, and the top reinforcement bars are resting directly on the bottom bars. The foreman says, 'Architect, it's fine, we will just pull the bars up with a hook while pouring.' What is your response?
o: Suggest adding extra bottom reinforcement to compensate for the displaced top bars.
Allow the pour but require a 7-day core test to verify the strength of that specific balcony.
Allow it, provided the foreman personally supervises the manual lifting of the bars during the pour.
Stop the pour immediately and require the installation of proper high-chairs or spacers to maintain the top bar position.
questions.n: In a cantilever, the tension is at the top; if the bars sink, the beam has zero leverage to resist gravity, leading to sudden failure.

questions.q: A concrete truck arrives at the site for a critical column pour. The delivery ticket shows the batch time was 120 minutes ago. The concrete looks fluid and hasn't started setting, but your specs strictly follow the 90-minute limit. The contractor offers to sign a waiver. As the Architect-of-Record, what do you do?
o: Accept the load but require the contractor to add a 'superplasticizer' to ensure it reaches the bottom of the column.
Reject the load and document the refusal in the site logbook.
Accept the load under the 'Waiver of Liability' signed by the contractor.
Accept the load if the slump test is within the 100mm limit.
questions.n: Adhering to the 90-minute rule (ASTM C94) ensures the chemical hydration process hasn't been compromised by heat or over-agitation.

questions.q: You are supervising the pouring of a massive 1.2-meter thick mat foundation. The contractor wants to use 'Type I' Ordinary Portland Cement because 'Type IV' (Low Heat) is out of stock. What is the primary risk you must address?
o: The concrete will not be strong enough to carry the building load.
The concrete will set too slowly, delaying the project.
The color of the concrete will be inconsistent with the rest of the structure.
Thermal cracking due to the high temperature difference between the core and the surface.
questions.n: Mass concrete generates immense internal heat; if the exterior cools too fast while the core stays hot, the concrete will tear itself apart.

questions.q: A client wants to change the floor finish from ceramic tiles to heavy 30mm thick granite slabs after the structural slabs have been poured. As the Architect, what is your first step?
o: Ask the Structural Engineer to re-calculate the slab capacity for the increased 'Dead Load.'
Approve the change as long as the client pays for the extra material cost.
Tell the contractor to use a thinner mortar bed to save weight.
Inform the client that changes are strictly prohibited after the slab is poured.
questions.n: Architects must coordinate changes that affect structural weight to ensure the Safety Factor is not compromised.

questions.q: You find 'Honeycombing' (exposed aggregate with voids) at the base of a newly stripped 4-meter high column. The contractor wants to 'patch it up with mortar' before the owner sees it. What is the correct procedure?
o: Ask the foreman why he didn't use enough water in the mix.
Order a non-destructive test (like Ultrasonic Pulse Velocity) to check the depth of the voids before deciding on a repair.
Immediately order the demolition of the column and a re-pour.
Allow the patch-up as long as they use high-strength non-shrink grout.
questions.n: You must determine if the honeycomb is just a 'surface' issue or if the entire base of the column is structurally compromised.

questions.q: You are inspecting the formwork for a second-story slab. You notice the contractor has used marine plywood that is slightly warped and has several visible gaps at the joints. The contractor argues that the 'slurry' will fill the gaps. What is your professional directive?
o: Request a higher slump concrete to ensure the gaps are completely filled by the aggregate.
Allow it, as long as the contractor agrees to plaster the ceiling later to hide the imperfections.
Reject the formwork and require all joints to be sealed with tape or foam to prevent mortar leakage.
Allow the pour but suggest a slightly thicker concrete mix to ensure it doesn't leak.
questions.n: Loss of mortar paste (slurry) through gaps leads to 'honeycombing' and sand streaks, significantly weakening the finished concrete surface.

questions.q: A massive beam is being poured, and a mechanical vibrator breaks down mid-pour. The contractor wants to continue by 'hand-puddling' with a piece of rebar. What is the most critical risk of this substitution?
o: The concrete will set too quickly for the rebar to be effective.
The rebar will scratch the epoxy coating of the structural steel.
The rebar will cause the concrete to segregate more than a vibrator would.
Inadequate consolidation leading to internal voids and poor bond with the reinforcement.
questions.n: Manual rodding cannot provide the high-frequency energy needed to liquefy the mix and ensure it fully encapsulates complex rebar cages.

questions.q: During the stripping of forms for a reinforced concrete wall, you notice several 'cold joints' where the two layers of concrete did not blend. The contractor claims it is purely aesthetic. How do you evaluate this?
o: It is only a problem if the joint is vertical rather than horizontal.
It is a structural defect because it creates a plane of weakness that can lead to water seepage and shear failure.
Accept it, but require the contractor to apply a waterproof membrane over the joint area.
It is purely aesthetic if the concrete was poured within the same day.
questions.n: Cold joints lack the monolithic bond required for the wall to act as a single structural unit, especially under lateral loads.

questions.q: You are the Architect of a high-end residence. The owner wants to remove a 'minor' concrete column in the kitchen to create an open-plan space. The contractor says, 'It's okay, we can just use a steel lintel.' What is your mandatory action?
o: Order the contractor to install the steel lintel immediately to satisfy the client's request.
Refuse the change until the Structural Engineer performs a formal load analysis and issues a revised structural plan.
Approve the change if the contractor provides a signed sketch of the steel lintel.
Allow it, but inform the owner that they must assume all risks for future ceiling cracks.
questions.n: Removing any vertical support alters the entire building's load distribution; this must be validated by the Engineer-of-Record.

questions.q: A concrete cylinder test report for a 28-day sample comes back at 85% of the required design strength. The building is already on its 4th floor. What is the most professional sequence of events?
o: Ignore the result, as concrete continues to gain strength for years after the 28-day mark.
Immediately order the demolition of all floors above the faulty pour.
Allow the project to continue but use higher-strength concrete for the remaining floors to compensate.
Conduct a Rebound Hammer test, followed by core sampling if necessary, to verify the actual in-place strength.
questions.n: Lab cylinders can fail due to poor handling; on-site testing confirms if the actual structure is deficient.

questions.q: In a residential project, the client insists on using 'River Stones' (smooth, round aggregates) for the structural concrete because they are cheaper. Why should you, as the Architect, discourage this for load-bearing members?
o: The smooth surface of the stone provides a poor mechanical bond with the cement paste compared to crushed angular stone.
Smooth aggregates provide better workability and are therefore acceptable for structural use.
River stones contain salt that will corrode the rebar.
River stones are too heavy and will increase the dead load of the slab significantly.
questions.n: Angular, crushed aggregate creates an interlocking matrix that is essential for high compressive and tensile performance.

questions.q: The contractor asks to use 'Bamboos' as temporary shoring (props) for a heavy concrete beam pour. What is your assessment based on standard safety practices?
o: Reject the use of bamboo as it is an organic material and its load capacity is unpredictable and inconsistent.
Allow it, provided the bamboo is green and freshly cut for maximum flexibility.
Allow the use of bamboo only if they are tied together in bundles of four.
Allow it for beams under 3 meters in span, as the load is minimal.
questions.n: Structural safety requires certified, predictable capacities (like steel or graded lumber) to prevent catastrophic formwork collapse.

questions.q: You are designing a beach-front villa. The owner wants 'fair-faced' (exposed) concrete walls. Which reinforcement specification is most critical to prevent future rust-staining on the facade?
o: Ensure a minimum concrete cover of 50mm to 70mm and specify galvanized or epoxy-coated rebar.
Increase the rebar size from 12mm to 16mm.
Specify a 'Broom Finish' to hide the cracks.
Use Type III High Early Strength cement.
questions.n: In coastal areas, chloride penetration is high; thick cover and protective coatings are the only ways to prevent the rebar from expanding and cracking the concrete face.

questions.q: During a concrete pour for a column, the 'form ties' snap, and the bottom of the formwork 'blows out.' The contractor wants to quickly push the concrete back in and re-secure the form. What is the danger?
o: The structural integrity is compromised by air entrapment, contamination with soil, and displacement of reinforcement.
The concrete will have lost its slump and will be too dry to finish.
The concrete will set faster due to the exposure to air.
The column will simply have a slight bulge that can be ground down later.
questions.n: Once a form 'blows,' the internal structure is ruined; the rebar has likely shifted, and the concrete is no longer monolithic.

questions.q: A contractor requests to use a 'Volumetric Mixer' (on-site mixing truck) instead of a traditional Ready-Mix truck for a remote project. What is the primary advantage of this system for a 'Division 03' specification?
o: It eliminates the '90-minute rule' risk because the concrete is mixed only when the truck arrives at the point of pour.
It allows the contractor to use any available local water source, including pond water.
It produces concrete that does not require any curing.
It is always cheaper than Ready-Mix concrete.
questions.n: Since materials are stored dry and mixed only at the nozzle or discharge, the concrete is always 'fresh' regardless of travel time.

questions.q: The contractor discovers a discrepancy between the Architectural Plans (showing a 200mm wall) and the Structural Plans (showing a 250mm wall) for a load-bearing partition. According to standard priority of documents, what is the correct first step?
o: Average the two dimensions and proceed with a 225mm wall to save time.
The contractor must notify the Architect in writing, who will then coordinate with the Structural Engineer to issue a clarification or Supplemental Instruction.
Follow the Structural Plans because they govern the safety of the building's skeleton.
Follow the Architectural Plans as the Architect is the prime professional.
questions.n: Formal notification ensures that the discrepancy is resolved by the professionals of record and documented for the final as-built drawings.

questions.q: A Project Specification mentions a specific brand of waterproof membrane 'or approved equal.' The contractor submits a cheaper alternative. What is the most critical factor you must verify before approving the 'equal'?
o: The contractor must provide a letter stating they will fix it if it leaks.
The alternative must have the same color and packaging as the specified brand.
The alternative must meet or exceed all performance criteria, such as hydrostatic pressure resistance and elongation, listed in the original spec.
The alternative must be manufactured in the same country as the original brand.
questions.n: The 'approved equal' status is strictly based on technical performance data and independent lab test results.

questions.q: During a site visit, you notice the contractor is using 'Re-rolled Steel' (rebars made from scrap) for the main structural columns instead of 'Billet-steel' bars. What is the immediate professional action?
o: Allow it if the contractor provides a discount to the owner.
Issue a 'Notice of Non-Compliance' and order the removal of the re-rolled bars from the site.
Allow it for the bottom half of the column where compression is highest.
Request a tension test for every single bar to prove they are strong enough.
questions.n: Re-rolled steel often lacks the ductility and consistent yield strength required by the Structural Code for seismic resistance.

questions.q: You are reviewing 'Division 01 - General Requirements.' The contractor has failed to submit the 'Construction Schedule' (PERT/CPM) three weeks after the start date. Why is this a major concern for the Architect?
o: The schedule is required only for the neighbors to know when the noise will stop.
The Architect cannot process the contractor's 'Request for Payment' without an approved schedule to track progress.
The Building Official will cancel the building permit if the schedule is missing.
The Architect needs the schedule to know when to take their vacation.
questions.n: Without a baseline schedule, the Architect has no objective way to verify the percentage of work accomplished for billing.

questions.q: A set of 'Proprietary Specifications' is used for the elevator system. During bidding, three contractors claim this is 'restrictive' and unfair. How do you defend this choice?
o: State that the owner simply likes the brand name.
Switch to a 'Prescriptive Specification' that describes the elevator's paint color instead.
Argue that this specific brand is the only one that fits the dimensions of the existing concrete shaft and meets the required speed.
Tell the contractors they are not allowed to complain about specifications.
questions.n: Proprietary specs are justified when a specific product is uniquely required for physical compatibility or specific performance needs.

questions.q: You are checking the 'Shop Drawings' for a complex steel staircase. You notice the fabricator changed the connection from 'Welded' to 'Bolted' for easier installation. What is your response?
o: Ask the fabricator to use both welding and bolting just to be safe.
Accept the change but tell the contractor they won't get extra pay for the bolts.
Approve it, as bolting is generally safer and faster on-site.
Return the drawing as 'Disapproved' or 'Revise and Resubmit' until the Structural Engineer validates the connection change.
questions.n: Architects 'review' shop drawings for design intent, but structural changes must be verified by the engineer who calculated the loads.

questions.q: A 'Prescriptive Specification' for a plaster wall describes the exact mix ratio (1 part cement to 3 parts sand). The finished wall is cracking. Who is primarily responsible if the contractor followed the ratio exactly?
o: The Architect/Specifier, because a prescriptive spec shifts the risk of the 'result' to the person who wrote the 'process.'
The Owner, for choosing a plaster finish instead of paint.
The Contractor, because they should have known the ratio was wrong.
The Sand Supplier, for providing sand that was too dry.
questions.n: In prescriptive specs, the designer guarantees that following the instructions will lead to the desired outcome.

questions.q: You are doing the 'Punch List' (Final Inspection) and find that the bathroom tiles are slightly uneven. The contractor claims it is within 'Industry Standards.' Where do you look to prove them wrong?
o: Measure the tiles with a standard ruler and hope for the best.
Look at the project's 'Division 09 - Finishes' specifications for 'Tolerances.'
Check the Building Permit to see if it mentions tile evenness.
Ask the owner if they are personally bothered by it.
questions.n: The specifications should define the maximum allowable 'lippage' or deviation for tile work in millimeters.

questions.q: A 'Performance Specification' for a glass curtain wall states it must withstand 250kph wind loads. The glass shatters during a 200kph storm. Who is primarily liable?
o: The Architect, for not picking a thicker glass.
The Client, for building the house in a windy area.
The Contractor/Manufacturer, because they failed to meet the specified performance criteria they were contracted to achieve.
The Wind, as it is considered an 'Act of God.'
questions.n: Performance specifications shift the 'design and choice' risk to the contractor to ensure the end result is met.

questions.q: The contractor submits an 'Application for Payment' that includes materials currently stored in their warehouse, not yet delivered to the site. According to most standard contracts, what should you do?
o: Disallow the payment for those specific items until they are 'On-Site' and verified, unless a specific 'Stored Materials' agreement is in place.
Pay for it immediately to help the contractor's cash flow.
Pay for it, but only if the contractor shows you a photo of the materials.
Ask the contractor to move the warehouse closer to the site.
questions.n: Standard practice limits payment to work 'placed in permanent position' or materials safely stored on the project site.

questions.q: You are designing a residential building on a lot with a significant slope. The client wants to maximize the floor area by building right up to the property line on the leeward side. According to the National Building Code (NBCP), what is the mandatory requirement for a wall built on a property line?
o: The wall must be painted with fire-retardant paint.
The wall must be a firewall with a minimum 2-hour fire-resistive rating and no openings (windows/doors).
You can have windows as long as they are made of tempered glass.
The wall must be at least 300mm thick regardless of the material used.
questions.n: Firewalls are designed to prevent fire spread between adjacent properties and must remain structurally intact even if one side collapses.

questions.q: A client asks you to sign and seal a set of architectural plans that were actually prepared by an unlicensed 'draftsman' to save on costs. The client assures you the design is perfect. What are the legal implications under R.A. 9266?
o: It is allowed if the draftsman is your full-time employee with a contract.
You can sign it but you should charge a higher fee for the 'risk' involved.
It is an act of 'signing and sealing' plans not prepared by the architect, which is grounds for suspension or revocation of your license.
It is acceptable as long as you review the plans and make minor corrections.
questions.n: Architects are legally responsible for the work they seal; sealing work by unlicensed individuals is a form of malpractice known as 'signing-in-blank.'

questions.q: You are determining the 'Total Gross Floor Area' (TGFA) for a project. The client wants to know if the unenclosed balconies and the basement parking count toward the Allowable Maximum Building Footprint (AMBF). How do you clarify this?
o: Basements never count toward any building bulk calculations.
Unenclosed balconies are always excluded from TGFA calculations.
Everything under a roof is part of the AMBF.
The AMBF is the actual land area occupied by the building at the ground level, while unenclosed spaces and basements have specific percentage deductions in TGFA.
questions.n: Zoning rules differentiate between what touches the ground (Footprint) and the total accumulated volume of the building (TGFA).

questions.q: During construction of a commercial building, the owner decides to change the occupancy of the second floor from 'Office' to 'Bar/Restaurant.' As the Architect, what is your most critical code concern?
o: The type of floor tiles used in the kitchen area.
The number of electrical outlets available for the DJ booth.
The Occupant Load Factor, which will likely increase, requiring wider stairs and more exit doors.
The color of the emergency exit signs.
questions.n: Bars and restaurants have higher density (fewer square meters per person) than offices, which triggers stricter fire safety and egress requirements.

questions.q: A contractor submits a request to use 'Medium Density Fiberboard' (MDF) for the built-in cabinets in a high-humidity area like a bathroom. Why should you reject this in your 'Division 06' (Wood and Plastics) review?
o: The wood grain of MDF doesn't look natural enough for a bathroom.
MDF is too expensive compared to marine plywood.
MDF is highly susceptible to moisture absorption, which causes swelling, warping, and mold growth in humid environments.
MDF is too heavy for standard cabinet hinges.
questions.n: Standard MDF lacks the water-resistance required for wet areas, leading to rapid material failure.

questions.q: In the 'Standard of Professional Practice' (SPP) Doc 202, what is the 'Multiple of Direct Personnel Expenses' method primarily used for?
o: Calculating the total cost of construction for a government project.
Determining professional fees for projects that require only technical research or consultation rather than full design.
A way to penalize contractors for being late on the schedule.
Calculating the number of bags of cement needed for a project.
questions.n: This method accounts for the time and overhead of specialized staff when the scope is non-standard or research-based.

questions.q: You are designing a cinema. The NBCP states that the 'Line of Sight' must be maintained. If the client wants to add more rows of seats without raising the floor height (raking), what is the technical consequence?
o: The project will be cheaper because it uses less concrete.
The acoustic quality of the cinema will improve.
The 'C-value' (clearance over the head of the person in front) will decrease, obstructing the view of the screen for rear rows.
The cinema will be safer because it is easier to walk on a flat floor.
questions.n: Proper cinema design requires a calculated slope (raking) to ensure every patron has an unobstructed view of the screen.

questions.q: A client wants to start construction 'immediately' using only your 'Design Development' drawings because the 'Working Drawings' are still 50% finished. What is your professional stance?
o: Allow it as long as the contractor is experienced enough to fill in the gaps.
Sign a waiver of liability so that any mistakes are the client's fault.
Advise the client that construction cannot proceed without 'Contract Documents' and a valid Building Permit, which requires 100% complete blueprints.
Tell the client to use a 'Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee' contract to make up for the missing details.
questions.n: Building permits and legal construction require 'For Construction' sets to ensure code compliance and builder accountability.

questions.q: In a project located near a fault line, the Structural Engineer specifies 'Ductile Detailing' for the concrete frames. As the Architect, how does this affect your site inspection of the rebar?
o: You will see fewer stirrups and ties to allow the concrete to move.
You should see closely spaced hoops and stirrups, especially at the beam-column joints, to prevent brittle failure during seismic shaking.
The rebar should be thinner and more flexible.
Rebar should only be placed in the center of the column to allow for swaying.
questions.n: Confinement reinforcement ensures the concrete doesn't explode (spall) and the rebar doesn't buckle under lateral loads.

questions.q: You are designing a public building and need to ensure compliance with BP 344 (The Accessibility Law). What is the maximum allowable gradient for a ramp?
questions.n: BP 344 strictly mandates a 1:12 ratio as the maximum slope for ramps to ensure safe accessibility.

questions.q: A project is nearing 95% completion, and the Owner wants to move furniture into the building. However, the 'Certificate of Occupancy' has not been issued yet. What is your directive as the Architect-of-Record?
o: Allow it as long as the furniture does not block the exits.
Ask the Contractor to sign a waiver of liability for the furniture.
Tell the Owner they can move in but must not use the elevators.
Advise the Owner that taking possession or occupying the building without a Certificate of Occupancy is a violation of the National Building Code.
questions.n: The Certificate of Occupancy is a legal clearance from the Building Official stating the structure is safe for its intended use.

questions.q: During a site walk-through, you notice the ramp for the disabled has a resting landing every 6 meters. However, the landing is only 1.20 meters long. Based on BP 344 (Accessibility Law), what is the deficiency?
o: The landing length is compliant, but the interval should be every 3 meters.
There is no deficiency; 1.20 meters is the standard door width.
The landing is too long; it should only be 1.00 meter.
The landing length should be a minimum of 1.50 meters to allow for wheelchair maneuvering and safety.
questions.n: BP 344 requires landings to have a minimum length of 1.50 meters to provide adequate space for a wheelchair to stop and turn.

questions.q: The Contractor submits a 'Change Order' request for a price escalation in steel bars, citing a sudden global market spike. The project is a 'Lump Sum' contract. How do you evaluate this request?
o: Tell the Contractor to use fewer bars to offset the price increase.
Reject the request because a Lump Sum contract fixed price includes the Contractor's risk for material price changes.
Ask the Owner to pay half of the difference to maintain a good relationship.
Automatically approve it because the market spike was outside the Contractor's control.
questions.n: Unless the contract explicitly allows for price adjustments due to inflation or market shifts, the bid price remains binding.

questions.q: You are reviewing the 'Division 01' specifications for 'Project Record Documents.' The Contractor asks why they need to maintain 'As-Built' drawings daily when they can just do it at the end of the project. What is your professional justification?
o: Daily updates ensure that 'hidden' utilities and structural changes are recorded accurately before they are covered by walls or slabs.
The Building Official needs to sign them every morning.
It is just a standard formality that looks good for the Owner.
It allows the Architect to bill the Owner for more supervision hours.
questions.n: Once components are 'built-in,' it is impossible to verify their exact location without destructive testing; real-time logging is essential.

questions.q: A project is located in a high-density residential zone (R-2). The Owner wants to build a roof deck with a high solid parapet wall that exceeds the 'Building Bulk' limits. What is the correct 'Rule 7/8' interpretation here?
o: Solid parapets are always exempted from height limits because they are for safety.
Allow it if the Owner pays a fine to the local homeowners association.
Explain that the parapet height must be included in the 'Established Grade' to 'Top of Roof' height measurement and must stay within the 'Allowable Building Height' (ABH).
Tell the Owner to build it and only deal with the issue if a neighbor complains.
questions.n: Building bulk is controlled by height limits and angles (Angular Planes) to ensure neighbors still receive light and ventilation.
